Bring what's due. Leave sure of it.

Margin lives inside a larger learning app, and it is more than a box for doubts. A student opens it with something due: tonight's homework, a textbook exercise, Friday's test. Margin gets her through it in her book's way, teaches her on the way, and remembers, so that tomorrow is easier and she comes back without being pushed.

The short answers

What should it feel like?

Useful in the first minute, from her own book, never a dead end, and always one clear next step. The favourite teacher who also knows her week.

Why do they come?

To get unstuck on one question that is due. Then to understand it, then to get ready for a test. In India, 73% of children who use AI use it for doubts and practice, and most of that is homework.

How do they find what it can do?

Inside the reply first, as her turn and a few choices; then one “next for you” card; the side panel when she wants more; the home screen when there is no question.

What brings them back?

The school week, not a guilt streak: what is due, what is fading, what sits underneath and what is coming. Daily use grows when the school, teacher and parent are in.

The product experience

The favourite teacher who also knows her week.

A good teacher answers the question you brought, the way the class does it, checks you can do the next one, notices what you keep getting wrong, and reminds you before the test. Margin should feel like that, on the phone, at 9 pm, every day. Below, each part of that experience: what it should be, why, and the features that deliver it. Some need features Margin does not have yet; they are marked.

Live in Margin today Partly live exists, needs extending New to build With school needs the school's week, a teacher or a parent
  1. 1

    It starts from her work, never from a blank box

    The camera, her chapter's questions and what is due tonight are on the first screen.

    Why

    The question is on paper in front of her. An empty chat box gives no clue what to ask. 73% of Indian children who use AI come with a doubt, mostly homework.

    Features that deliver it
    • NewCamera-first home: snap a question, a page or her working
    • NewStarter questions from the chapter she is on
    • NewScan a textbook page and tap the part she is stuck on
    • Partly liveType, or speak in English, Hindi or Hinglish
    • With school“Due tomorrow”, from a diary photo or the school
  2. 2

    It is useful in the first minute

    No sign-up, no tour, no setting to choose. The first answer arrives in seconds.

    Why

    Moving sign-up after the first lesson raised Duolingo's daily users by about 20%. A first reply slower than Google Lens loses a child on day one; Margin took 10.9 seconds to its first words on 18 November.

    Features that deliver it
    • NewClass and book taken from the app's profile
    • NewVetted answers served from the bank: first words in under 3 seconds
    • New“I read:” shown before the answer, with Edit
  3. 3

    Her book, her teacher's way

    The answer uses the method, the page and the picture from her NCERT book, prepared and checked by subject experts.

    Why

    Her teacher marks her notebook. A right answer in another method is a wrong answer to her, and to her parent.

    Features that deliver it
    • LiveThe book's method and page in every reply
    • LiveThe book's picture, drawn with her question's numbers
    • Partly liveA bank of answers checked by subject experts
    • NewRemember the method she chose for the chapter
    • With schoolHer teacher's notes and steps as a source
  4. 4

    It gets her through tonight, and teaches on the way

    Margin decides between the answer and guided steps, and she always has a way to the full working.

    Why

    Students stopped using a tutor that only gave hints (Khanmigo, Tennessee, 2026). In a 334-student trial, free access beat “read first, then ask”. Homework must get done.

    Features that deliver it
    • Partly liveGuided step by step, chosen per question by Margin
    • NewChecks inside the steps: fill in the blank, find the wrong statement
    • NewCheck my work: the wrong line found from a notebook photo
    • NewMarks the way a paper checker gives them
    • With schoolHomework locked to steps by a parent or teacher
  5. 5

    She sees one next thing, not everything

    Her turn and a few choices inside the reply, one “next for you” card after it, the library only when she pulls it up.

    Why

    Suggestions placed under an answer are the ones people use; generic ones and walls of links are ignored. A child does not choose well among six kinds of resource.

    Features that deliver it
    • LiveA question for her at the end of every reply
    • LiveThe side panel: videos, labs, games, practice, mix-ups
    • NewOne “next for you” card, chosen from her answer
    • NewChips under the reply: step by step, check mine, Hindi
    • NewAsk from a paused video, at that second
  6. 6

    She has a reason to come back every day

    The home screen is her week: what is due, what is fading, what sits underneath, what is coming.

    Why

    A study app cannot count on a doubt every day. Short daily units and streaks that forgive built Duolingo's habit; ChatGPT's proactive daily brief, with no real reason behind it, was retired.

    Features that deliver it
    • NewSpaced review: a new question on the right day
    • NewGaps read from her doubts, fixed with a short path
    • NewHome cards, at most four, each saying why
    • NewA test plan from a date; a streak that counts learning
    • With schoolWarm-ups from the timetable; plans from test dates
  7. 7

    It is never a dead end

    Every kind of failure has its own way out, and a person stands behind the machine.

    Why

    Under 1% of people press thumbs-down, so errors must be found by checking. PhysicsWallah puts a human expert behind its AI. A doubt limit in the middle of homework loses her.

    Features that deliver it
    • New“Not how my teacher did it”: the book's other method
    • NewSmaller steps, then a mentor from the app
    • NewOne tap to flag; flagged answers go back to subject experts
    • Partly liveCost under ₹1 a doubt, so no doubt limit
  8. 8

    It is honest with the family

    One weekly page of what she can now do, the same for her and her parent, including when an answer was shown instead of taught.

    Why

    The parent often owns the phone and pays. 54% of urban parents limit screen time, and many distrust education apps after the refund and mis-selling complaints of past years.

    Features that deliver it
    • NewThe week's page, shared with the parent
    • NewTold when answers were shown; she is told first
    • NewConsent for memory across classes, and erase
    • NewStudy hours and a quiet time
    • NewA milestone card to share, with no marks

Why they come

Nobody opens a study app for AI. They open it because something is due and they are stuck.

Surveys of Indian and American students agree on the order. The first reason is one specific question, usually homework or a textbook exercise. Understanding comes second, getting ready for a test third. Underneath all of them is a feeling: no one nearby can help, and asking in class feels risky.

  1. 1

    Get unstuck on this question, tonight

    Homework, a textbook exercise, a question from class. In India, 73% of children who use AI use it for “doubt solving and practice”, and the survey says that includes finishing homework. Maths is the top subject. In the US, 43% of teens use chatbots to solve maths problems.

    73%of Indian children using AI, for doubts and practice

  2. 2

    Understand it, in words that make sense

    The top reason Indian children keep using AI is “easy-to-understand explanations” (45%), then quick answers (41%), “feels like chatting with a person” (40%) and being able to ask a follow-up (35%).

    45%keep using AI for its explanations

  3. 3

    Be ready for the test

    32% of Indian children who use AI use it to prepare for tests; among users of learning apps it is 47%. In Class 10, the board exam sets the whole year.

    47%of learning-app users, for test preparation

  4. 4

    Check that I got it right

    Google says 75% of Photomath users check their own answers with it; the claim is undated. Before a test this is the main job: “is my working right, and where would I lose marks?”

    75%Photomath's own claim, undated

  5. 5

    Look something up, or follow a curiosity

    48% of US teens research topics with AI; 25% of Indian children who use AI ask out of curiosity. This is a smaller reason to open a study app, and the general assistants serve it well.

    25%of Indian AI users, for curiosity

Indian figures from the Bharat Survey for EdTech 2025 (Central Square Foundation; 12,500 children from low-income homes in ten states, fieldwork July 2025 to January 2026). US figures from Pew Research, 24 February 2026. The groups differ, so the percentages are not a single ranking; the order is the same in every survey found.

When

In the evening, after school and tuition, and just before a deadline. In the only hourly data found (a US university course), 47% of help requests came between 7 pm and midnight. Use rises and falls with the school year and peaks before exams.

Where they go now

YouTube (94%), WhatsApp (67%) and Google (49%). Only 6% use a dedicated learning app. And 63% started using any learning technology because a school or teacher recommended it.

How they feel

28% of 3.79 lakh students say they hesitate to ask questions in class. A Class 10 student said: “There is a fear of asking doubts to teachers. But AI feels like a friend and helps us.” 87% get help at home, mostly from mothers, who can often supervise but not explain the maths.

So the first thing Margin must do well is take the exact question in front of her and get her through it, kindly and fast.

Explaining, checking, review and plans are all earned by doing that first job better than YouTube, Google Lens and ChatGPT. And because most children start using learning tools when a school or teacher recommends them, the school is not an extra. It is a door.

Sources: BaSE 2025 report · Central Square Foundation, 24 Feb 2026 · Pew, 24 Feb 2026 · SIGCSE 2022 · NCERT survey via Careers360. Full notes: research_notes/Product experience 2026-11-25/why-students-come.md.

The student

A CBSE student loves a teacher who gets them through the exam, on the phone they already hold.

Their real study tools today are YouTube teachers, Google Lens and a parent's phone in the evening. What they value is tied to marks. What they and their parents reject is anything that blocks tonight's homework, shows ads or pushes a sale.

Their favourite teacher, on YouTube

143.5M subscribers across PhysicsWallah's 379 YouTube channels

Students subscribe widely but watch only the chapter they need: Magnet Brains has 14.6 million subscribers and averages about 9,300 views a video. A Class 10 maths one-shot by Shobhit Nirwan has 11 million views.

For Margin: sound like a favourite teacher, not a search engine. Offer the two minutes of video that answer the doubt, and a full revision video only when asked.

Multibagg, 17 Nov 2026 · Qoruz, Nov 2026

Point the phone at the problem

61% of urban 10 to 16 year olds who use AI use it for homework

54% of urban children aged 10 to 16 use AI tools, and 67% of them say they turn to AI because their parents are too busy. Google says India uses Lens more each month than any other country, with education a top use.

For Margin: the camera is the front door. Typing a maths question on a phone is the obstacle.

vivo and CMR, Dec 2025

Marks, and being ready for the test

81% of 3.79 lakh students named studies and exams as their main worry

Sample papers, previous years' questions, the marking scheme and “important questions” are what they search for. 27% of students take private coaching, 38% at secondary level. Asked what maths help they want, 54% of urban parents said “more regular practice”.

For Margin: connect every question to the test: how marks are given, a similar past-paper question, “ready for Friday”.

NCERT survey, 2022 data · government education survey, 2025 · The Week, 23 Oct 2026

Hinglish, and a teacher who talks like them

13% of low-income children learning with technology say content is not in their language

The large free channels keep separate Hindi-medium and English-medium channels. Urban Hindi speakers often type to AI in Hinglish, and models follow instructions less well in mixed Hindi and English.

For Margin: accept Hinglish, reply in the language of the question, keep the written maths in the form the exam expects.

JMIR, 2026

Games, streaks and being seen

77.4M monthly players of Free Fire in India

In Peru, a streak feature raised both use and maths scores among 60,000 children in Grades 4 to 6. In India, a reading contest with a leaderboard raised stories read by about 45%, and the effect partly lasted after prizes ended.

For Margin: streaks that count learning and can be repaired; recognition from the teacher and the parent; word problems in worlds they like, such as cricket.

IPR working paper, Feb 2026 · arXiv 2310.10850 · TechCrunch, 28 Oct 2026

A phone that is often a parent's

54% of urban parents limit their child's screen time

About two thirds of 57,000 urban parents call their child addicted to social media, video or games. Yet only 26% of Indians want AI banned in schools, against 78% who want social media banned for under-14s.

For Margin: the parent is allowed to like this app. Be light on data, resume where she stopped, and leave the parent a short, honest note.

LocalCircles, Dec 2025 · Ipsos, 31 Aug 2026

What puts them off

  • Hints that never end. In a 2026 Tennessee trial, students ignored or argued with Khanmigo when it only gave hints.
  • A cap in the middle of homework. “Doubts Exhausted” after two questions, as we saw on Infinity Learn.
  • Ads and sales calls. Indian parents still distrust education apps after the refund and mis-selling complaints of 2021 and 2022.
  • Being made to type a maths question with fractions and symbols on a phone keyboard.
  • Long lectures when they wanted one line, though they choose two-hour revision videos the night before an exam.

Why students pick a particular YouTube teacher has no Indian survey behind it; it rests on how the channels describe themselves. No nationwide survey of AI use by 9 to 16 year olds exists yet. Full notes and sources: research_notes/Product experience 2026-11-25/what-cbse-students-love.md.

Cues from those who came before

Earlier startups show what fails. The best products show what keeps people.

Each lesson below changed something in Margin's experience. The startup lessons come from what happened to the products, not only to their finances.

DoubtnutValued near $150M, sold for about $10M

Snap a photo, get a video solution, free. It built huge reach, but the answer was all it gave. Nothing brought a student back except the next doubt, and ChatGPT then gave the same answer for free.

For Margin: the answer gets her in. What happens after it, and on the days with no doubt, is the product.

Finshots, Dec 2023

CheggStaff cut by about 45% in Oct 2025

A paid bank of answers. When free assistants and AI answers in search gave answers too, the reason to pay was gone.

For Margin: an answer alone is free everywhere. Charge, if ever, for what is hers: her book, her week, her progress.

Company filings; see the 17 November market notes

Snapchat My AI75% one-star reviews in a week

Pinned at the top of every user's chats, with no way to remove it.

For Margin: inside the larger app, Margin is offered where it helps, never forced onto screens where it is not wanted.

TechCrunch, Apr 2023

Duolingo64.9M daily users, up 29% in a year

A lesson before sign-up raised daily users about 20%. A short daily unit anyone can finish. Streaks that can be repaired. Hundreds of small tests, each worth one to four per cent.

For Margin: value before any set-up; a two-minute daily unit; a streak that forgives; test everything in small steps.

Duolingo Q3 2026 letter · Duolingo blog

PhysicsWallahAI Guru: about 4.5M doubts a month

A teacher students already love, prices families can pay, and an AI that answers about 90% of doubts, with a human expert when a student marks an answer wrong.

For Margin: trust comes from people the student already knows. A person stands behind the machine.

Business Today, 1 Jun 2026

What the chat products have learnt

The question of what an AI tutor should feel like is the same one ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude face.

The blank box fails

An empty chat box gives no clue what to ask. Broad example prompts help; narrow ones and early tips are ignored.

NN/g, Mar 2024

Follow-ups under the answer work best

Of all prompt suggestions, the ones placed under an answer are the most useful. Generic ones are ignored.

NN/g, Apr 2025

Modes a user must find go unused

Study modes sit behind a switch. OpenAI has published no figure on how many students turn it on.

General assistants notes, 16 Nov 2026

Reaching out needs a reason

ChatGPT's proactive daily brief, Pulse, launched in September 2025 and was retired in June 2026, replaced by tasks users set themselves.

OpenAI Help

Few people press thumbs-down

Explicit feedback came on under 1% of interactions in one study. Errors must be found by checking, not by waiting for complaints.

arXiv 2509.18361

Locking answers away backfires

Students who could use AI freely did better than those made to read first (0.21 SD, 334 students). University students mostly ask for answers and skip about half of the hints.

IZA, Dec 2025 · arXiv 2604.23486

Where students go today, and where each one stops

Each of these does one thing well. None of them is a tutor.

A video

A good teacher explaining, as many times as the student wants to watch.

What a video cannot do

  • Hear the student's question
  • Find the two minutes that matter in a ten-minute lesson
  • Notice where the student got lost
  • Check that anything was understood
What would a tutor do with the same video?See what Margin does

What Margin does

  • Answers the doubt first, in words and a picture
  • Opens the video at the part that explains this doubt
  • Asks a question afterwards to see if it landed

A solved answer

A solutions page, an answer app or a chatbot. It gets tonight's homework done.

What solving the question alone cannot do

  • Say where the student's own working went wrong
  • Hold back when one hint would be enough
  • Follow the method the student's book uses
  • Check the student can do the next one alone
What would a tutor do with the same question?See what Margin does

What Margin does

  • Finds the step the student missed and names it
  • Gives one hint and waits, or the full working, as the doubt needs
  • Uses the textbook's method and shows the page
  • Ends with a fresh question to try

A game or a simulation

It makes a student want to try, and lets them change a number and watch what happens.

What playing alone cannot do

  • Explain what the student just saw
  • Know that this is the moment it is needed
  • Link the play to the working in the notebook
  • Answer when the student asks why
What would a tutor do with the same game?See what Margin does

What Margin does

  • Brings in the right game or simulation for this doubt
  • Tells the student what to change and what to look for
  • Ties what they saw back to the method and the page

A tutor does all of this at once

Software that responds at every step of a student's working teaches about as well as a human tutor in controlled studies. Software that only marks the final answer does less than half as well.

Margin is an AI-powered tutor.

Why a chat tutor

A video, a simulation or a game does much less on its own. Each needs teaching around it, and the reply is that teaching.

The alternative to a chat is easy to state: skip the conversation and send each child the right video, simulation or game. It has been tried in universities, in schools and through messages sent home. The result repeats.

The rows come from different studies, ages and subjects, and are not a ranking of video against games. Watching also feels like learning when it is not: physics students rated a polished lecture above an active class and learned less from it (Deslauriers and others, 2019).

The direct test, published three weeks ago

Google and Eedi ran the comparison this question asks for. In ten state schools in the United Kingdom, 1,179 pupils in Years 8 to 10 worked through maths for ten weeks. After a wrong answer, one group got curated videos and hints written by experts. The others got a chat with a tutor, human or AI.

Fixed the mistake on the next try

From the smaller study of 2025.

From the ten-week trial of 2026.

Chat with an AI tutortwo versions; each message approved by a person
59.0% and 59.9%

A person approved each AI message before it was sent, and passed 94.7% of them unchanged. Source: LearnLM team at Google and Eedi, December 2025 and 29 October 2026.

The limit, from the same trial: a chat repairs the doubt. It does not cover the chapter faster.

On a broad maths test after ten weeks, the tutored pupils did no better than the group on videos and hints (−0.01 and +0.02 standard deviations). They had worked through fewer units, because a conversation takes longer than a hint. So the claim to make for Margin is specific: it is the best way to fix the doubt in hand, and it supplies the teaching that videos, simulations and games need around them. It also means Margin has to keep the child moving through the chapter.

A chat can also fail. Three ways it has.

The method is not safe by default. Each of these was a real product in a real study.

−17%

As an answer machine

An open chat that gives the answer raised practice scores and cut the later exam score.

Bastani and others, 2025

17%

As a button beside the work

In 18 Tennessee middle schools the median student messaged the tutor in 17% of the sessions where they made a mistake. Gains matched practice without AI.

Oreopoulos and Low, 2026, on Khanmigo

−0.37

As open access with no structure

University course sections that were given an AI tutor finished with lower final grades than sections without it.

University of Maryland, October 2026

Why this method, then

Three things a chat does that a library of resources cannot.

It answers the child's own attempt

Feedback that explains is worth 0.49. Feedback that only marks right or wrong is worth 0.05. Only a reply can explain the slip this child has just made.

0.49against 0.05, 40 studies

Van der Kleij, Feskens and Eggen, 2015

It chooses, so the child does not have to

Letting learners decide what to study next adds 0.05, close to nothing. Left alone, students pick what feels easy. A tutor that has just seen the child's answer is placed to choose better.

0.05from learner control, 18 studies

Karich, Burns and Maki, 2014

It is how these children already ask

Of low-income Indian children who learn with technology, 77% use it to practise and clear doubts, and 35% already use generative AI, most of them every day. What keeps those children using it: easy explanations, quick answers, and that it “feels like chatting with a person”.

45%easy explanations41%quick answers40%like chatting with a person

BaSE 2025, 12,500 households

So the experience has to do six things

These are the conditions under which chat tutoring has worked. The journey and the side panel below put them into practice.

Be the way through the work

Open Margin from every question, exercise and video, with the page and the question already attached. A tutor that waits to be called goes unused.

Teach from checked content

Every trial with a gain held a prepared solution, a scripted lesson or a person approving messages. Margin's vetted Methods and reviewed bank are that.

End every reply with a turn for the student

The child answers one question. The reply to that answer is where most of the teaching happens.

Choose the next step

One recommended step, picked from what the child just did. Not a menu.

Give less as the child succeeds

Full working helps a beginner (+0.505) and holds back a child who already knows the idea (−0.428).

Keep the child moving, and bring the question back

Always show the way on to the next idea. Ask the same question again in a few days. That is also how to measure Margin.

The journey, screen by screen

Six moments decide whether a student stays.

Riya is in Class 8 at a CBSE school and already uses the app for its videos. Tonight she has maths homework from Chapter 1, Fractions in Disguise. These are the moments she meets Margin, from the first tap to the week she decides it is hers. The screens are prototypes in the live app's style.

  1. 1First openWhat is here for me?
  2. 2First answerDid that help, fast?
  3. 3Finding moreWhat else can it do?
  4. 4Something goes wrongCan I trust it?
  5. 5Every dayWhy open it today?
  6. 6Deciding to stayIs this worth it?
Moment 1 · First open

She opens it with homework in her hand. The first screen asks for the homework, not for a prompt.

No sign-up, no tour, no blank box. The larger app already knows her class and book, so Margin opens on her chapter. The biggest target is the camera, because the question is usually on paper in front of her. Below it sit three real questions from the chapter she is on: tapping one is the fastest way to see what a reply looks like.

The three “It can also” tiles are the menu. They name jobs she already has, in her words. They teach what Margin does without a tutorial, and each opens a different kind of help.

  • Goal: something useful on screen within a minute of the first tap.
  • Language is a one-tap choice in the top bar, not a setting.
Moment 2 · First answer

The first reply has to be fast, from her book, and end with something for her to do.

Exercise 1.1, Q4p. 7
I read: “Three quarters of my paint mixture is red. What percentage is red?”Edit

Same as Example 1 in your book pp. 1–2. Per cent means “out of 100”, so make 100 parts:

red

¾ = 6⁄8 = 30⁄40 = 75⁄100 = 75%

The paint does not change. We only count it in smaller parts.

Your turn: ⅖ of a mixture is blue. What per cent?

25%40%52%
Step by step Check mineहिंदी में

“I read” comes first. Photo solvers that show what they read let the student fix a misread before it spoils the answer. It is the cheapest trust a reply can earn.

The reply is the book's working, kept short: the page, one picture, the chain of equal fractions the book uses, and one sentence of meaning. These are the four parts every reply has.

It ends with her turn. A question she answers with a tap, then three chips that are the other ways Margin can help with this same question.

Speed is part of the experience. In the 18 November test Margin took 10.9 seconds to its first words on this question. A first reply that feels slower than Google Lens loses a child on day one. Target: first words in under three seconds, with vetted answers served straight from the bank.
Moment 3 · Finding more

She learns what exists one step at a time, at the moment it is useful.

    Right after it: one “Next for you” card, chosen from how she answered. One choice, not fifteen.
  3. 3
    Pulled up when wanted: “More on this” holds videos, labs, games, practice and mix-ups. It is a bottom sheet on a phone and a side panel on a laptop. It is the shelf, not the front door.
  4. 4
    On the home screen: what to do next, when there is no question in hand (Moment 5).

New things are shown once, when they fit. The first time she types out her own working, Margin offers: “Snap your notebook next time and I'll find the line that went wrong.” A feature met at the moment it would have helped is remembered; a feature in a tour is not.

Moment 4 · Something goes wrong

When it disagrees with her teacher, or she is still stuck, there is always a next move.

Every kind of failure has its own way out.

  • Still stuck after the explanationDrop to smaller steps and ask her to fill in one part, then offer a person: the app's mentor.
  • A wrong answer from MarginOne tap to flag it; a flagged vetted answer goes back to the subject experts.
  • Out of free doubtsNever mid-homework. Infinity Learn's “Doubts Exhausted” screen in our test is the opposite of this.

The home screen is the reason to open it on a day with no doubt. At most four cards, each saying why it is there:

  • What is due, from a diary photo, or from the school when it is connected.
  • What is fading: spaced review, always a new question, on the right day.
  • What sits underneath: the gap behind repeated doubts, as a short path.
  • What is coming: a test date turns into a plan.

The streak counts days she made something sure, a review answered or a doubt closed with her own correct answer. It does not count minutes or app opens. It sits small in the corner, and missing a day does not reset it to zero.

Ready for Friday: 80%

A student keeps an app that makes her feel more capable. The weekly page counts what she now knows, in the chapter's own words, not minutes or messages.

The parent is the second decision-maker. In India the parent often owns the phone and pays. A short, honest weekly view, including when Margin gave an answer instead of teaching it, is what keeps the app installed.

“Ready for Friday” turns practice into a number she cares about: marks on the next test.

What brings her back

Five loops bring her back. The school's week is the strongest.

A study app cannot count on a doubt every day. It needs reasons that recur on their own. Each loop below starts from something real in her life, so a reminder is a help, not a nag.

The school week

Homework every evening, a class tomorrow, a test on Friday. The trigger comes from school, so Margin only has to be the easiest place to act on it.

Strongest · grows when the school is in

What is fading

Two minutes of spaced review: one new question on something learnt days ago, on the day it would start to slip.

Daily · works on her own

Visible progress

The week's page, “ready for Friday: 80%”, a gap marked fixed. She can see herself getting better.

Weekly · works on her own

People who notice

A teacher who sets homework through Margin, a parent who praises the week's page, a mentor who calls when she is stuck.

Grows with teacher and parent

Fun with a point

The app's games and labs after a doubt, a streak that forgives, class contests, word problems set in cricket or her favourite game.

Keeps it light

One ordinary week, and why she opens Margin each day

SunNothing asked of her

Should she spend more time in it?

More minutes is the wrong goal. A child who spends an hour stuck in Margin has had a bad evening, and a parent shown minutes learns nothing about whether she is getting better.

The right goal is more of her study going through Margin: homework, review, test plans, and the app's videos and games reached from a reply. Time grows as a result, and every minute is one a parent is glad of.

Reminders, with rules

At most one a day, only for something real (due, fading, a test), never in quiet hours the parent sets. No guilt wording, and no message about a broken streak.

Why: Duolingo's own tests found the right reminder adds a few per cent of retention, while a 2025 review of children's apps flagged its “excessive notifications”. For children, the parent decides whether the app stays.

Read across the tables

Group A carries Open, Find and Recover: a student alone gets a good tutor. Daily and Stay get much stronger as B, C and D join, because a reason to come back every day comes from the school's week, and the decision to keep the app is made partly by the parent. The B2C product is the base. The school and the family are what make it a habit.

The side panel

Lead with one next step.

The order of the panel is a teaching decision. The top of a list gets used most, and a child does not choose well among six kinds of resource.

The proposed order runs from watching, to playing, to working. It is the right path for one child: the one who did not follow the explanation. For the child who did follow it, the first three places go to the items that ask least of them, and practice, which has the strongest evidence at school age, comes fourth.

More for this idea, one of each

1
Practise was 4thThree questions, mixed with earlier kinds, then a check that explains. Mixed practice: 61% against 38% on a surprise test a month later.
2
Common mix-ups was 5th, split outThe wrong working beside the right one. Text that names and corrects a wrong idea adds 0.41.
3
Try it was 2ndThe simulation, with a prediction asked first. Guided exploring beats unguided by 0.50.
4
Watch was 1stThe two-minute clip as a second explanation, with a question after it.
5

6

Sources: Rohrer and others, 2020 (54 Class 7 classes). Lazonder and Harmsen, 2016. Clark, Tanner-Smith and Killingsworth, 2016. Schroeder and Kucera, 2022. Larwin, Gorman and Larwin, 2013.

Why order matters, and why this one

Wherever position has been measured, the first place draws the most use, and a recommendation draws more still.

+33%

more views for whichever item came first in a weekly list whose order was random.

Feenberg and others, 2017

10.5%

of clicks went to the first of six links and 7.3% to the fifth, with the same links rotated through each place.

Murphy, Hofacker and Mizerski, 2006

0.68

is how far an option chosen in advance shifts what people pick, across 58 studies. It works best when it reads as a recommendation.

Jachimowicz and others, 2019

None of these comes from children using a learning product. The direction is not in doubt. The size of the effect in Margin is unknown until it is measured there.

Why not video first

For a child who followed the explanation, a video repeats what they know. Margin can tell that child from the one who is still lost by the answer to the closing question, so the video goes to the top exactly when it is needed.

Why practice first

It works for both children. It proves the idea to the one who has it, and it shows the gap to the one who has not, with a check that explains. Common mix-ups come second: a short correction of a wrong idea takes seconds and has good evidence.

Why the game moves back

A game is a weak next step straight after a doubt and a good habit across a week. Class 7 and 8 pupils enjoyed an algebra game more than a step-by-step tutor and learned less from it.

Long and Aleven, 2017

How the top card is chosen

Margin knows one thing at this moment that no library knows: whether the child got the closing question right.

The question at the end of the replyThree choices to tap. The answer decides the card.
Answered right

Make it stick

  1. Three more, mixed with last week's kinds.
  2. Play the game this week, for speed.
  3. On to the next idea in the chapter.
Answered wrong

Repair it

  1. The slip beside the right working, inside the reply.
  2. Watch two minutes, or try it in the simulation.
  3. Wrong again: the step before this one, from the learning path.
No answer

Bring it back

  1. The card stays on the same question, one tap to answer.
  2. Tomorrow the question returns in a reminder.
  3. The rest of the panel keeps its order.

The order bends with what the student came for

The six kinds of request from the pitch, and one more. These are design proposals that follow from the evidence above. They have not been tested as a set.

The student came toTop of the panelWhy
Understand a conceptTry it, then WatchA new idea needs to be seen moving. The simulation asks for a prediction first.
Clear a doubtPractise after a right answer, Watch after a wrong oneThe answer to the closing question says which child this is.
Solve a problemOne more like itFor a beginner, an example followed by a problem beats problems alone.
Get one hint for homeworkNothing. The panel stays closedThe child asked to do the work. Anything more gives it away.
Check an answerThe mix-up that matches the slipThe gain comes from answering the child's own error.
PractisePractise, then PlayQuestions first, the game as the way to get fast.
Revise for a test tomorrowCommon mix-ups, formulas, mixed practiceA formula sheet helps while it is open. Mixed questions show what is still shaky.

Three changes to the panel itself

One of each, not fifteen

The panel in the pitch screenshot lists more than fifteen items. Show the best one of each kind and keep the rest behind “more”. Too many options hurt most when the choice is hard and the chooser is unsure, which describes a nine-year-old.

Chernev, Böckenholt and Goodman, 2015

Labels that say the need

“Still not clear? Watch two minutes” tells a child more than “Videos”. Name each row by what the child wants to do, not by the kind of file.

Split formulas from mix-ups

A mix-up is a correction with evidence behind it. A formula sheet is a reference. When the child's own answer shows a known mix-up, the correction belongs inside the reply.

What nobody has tested

No study has tested the order of follow-on resources after a tutor's reply, in any product or age group. The order here is assembled from the evidence on each item. Margin can settle it with a rotation test over a few weeks: show different orders to different students, then compare how they answer the same question a week later and how many units of the chapter they cover. Not clicks, and not watch time.

It knows when

And when the question is new

Students change the numbers, mix two chapters and ask things no teacher wrote down. Margin has a route for each case, and every route ends in the bank.

A question it knows

The vetted answer for this book, class and kind of help is shown as it is, with its page, picture and media.

A familiar idea with new numbers

The expert's method is reused. The maths is worked again for the new numbers and checked, and the picture is redrawn.

A doubt nobody has asked before

A low-cost frontier model answers from the textbook and credible sources, inside the same guardrails. The first answer can take a little longer.

Every new answer is stored, checked by experts and reused. The bank grows each time a student asks.

Lakhs of questions

A question bank tagged chapter by chapter, with the textbook's own exercises at the centre.

A hundred items a chapter

About a hundred videos, labs, games and practice items are linked to each chapter that is live, each tied to the idea it teaches.

Every Indian board

Built to cover CBSE, ICSE and ISC, and the state boards, book by book.

Then five more questions, in Class 4 and Class 8

Each was put to three frontier models, two Indian doubt-solving apps and Margin. Pick a question to read what each one said.Each question follows, with what each one said.

Question 1 of 5

I’m in Class 4. My friend says one eighth of a roti is bigger than one quarter because 8 is bigger than 4. Our rotis are the same size. Is my friend right?

Frontier models

GPT-6.2 AstraFrontier model
No. One quarter of a roti is bigger than one eighth when the rotis are the same size. Imagine cutting your roti into 4 equal pieces. Each piece is one quarter. Now cut each piece in half. You have 8 equal pieces, and each one is smaller. So two eighths of the roti make one quarter. The 8 tells you how many equal pieces the roti was cut into.

Text only

Claude Opus 5.5Frontier model
No, your friend is not right. One quarter is bigger than one eighth. One quarter (1/4): cut the roti into 4 equal pieces and take 1 piece. One eighth (1/8): cut the same roti into 8 equal pieces and take 1 piece. When you cut the roti into more pieces, each piece gets smaller. …
1/4 of a roti:  [  piece  ][        ][        ][        ]
1/8 of a roti:  [pc][  ][  ][  ][  ][  ][  ][  ]

Text, with a sketch typed in characters

Gemini 4 HydrogenFrontier model
Imagine you have two rotis that are the exact same size. To make one quarter, you cut the first roti into 4 equal pieces and take 1 piece. To make one eighth, you cut the second roti into 8 equal pieces and take 1 piece. … one quarter is bigger than one eighth, which means your friend is not right.

Text only

Indian doubt-solving apps

Vedantu Ask VedDoubt-solving app
Oh, that’s a classic puzzle! Your friend is actually not right, even though it sounds like it should be true because 8 is bigger than 4. Think of it this way: if you have one roti and you share it with 4 friends, everyone gets a nice, big piece. But if you have to share that same roti with 8 friends, you have to cut it into much smaller pieces so everyone gets some! … Does that make sense, or would you like to see a drawing of how that works?

Text. Offers a drawing if the student asks

Infinity Learn DoubtsDoubt-solving app
Hint: Imagine you have one whole yummy roti. If you cut it into pieces, what happens to the size of each piece as you make more cuts? Solution steps 1 to 4 … Solution: No, your friend is not right. One quarter of a roti is bigger than one eighth of a roti because when you cut a whole roti into fewer equal pieces, each piece is bigger.

Text. The hint, four steps and the answer appear together

Margin

MarginFrom the student’s own textbook
No. One quarter of a roti is bigger than one eighth when the rotis are the same size. Look at these two same-size rotis. One piece is coloured in each. The 8 tells us that the roti is cut into 8 equal pieces. The 4 tells us it is cut into 4 equal pieces. When the same-size roti is cut into more pieces, each piece is smaller. … Your turn: One roti is shared equally by 3 friends, and a same-size roti by 6 friends. Who gets the bigger piece?

Question 2 of 5

I’m in Class 4. I shared 3 rotis equally between 4 children. How much did each child get?

Frontier models

GPT-6.2 AstraFrontier model
Each child got ¾ of a roti. Cut each roti into 4 equal pieces and give each child one piece from each roti. Each child gets 3 quarter-pieces, which makes ¾ of a roti.

Text only

Claude Opus 5.5Frontier model
Each child got 3/4 (three-quarters) of a roti. 1. Cut each roti into 4 equal pieces (one piece for each child). 2. Each piece is 1/4 of a roti. 3. 3 rotis × 4 pieces = 12 pieces in total. 4. Share 12 pieces among 4 children: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 pieces each. 5. 3 pieces of 1/4 each = 3/4 of a roti.
Roti 1:  [A][B][C][D]
Roti 2:  [A][B][C][D]
Roti 3:  [A][B][C][D]

Gemini 4 HydrogenFrontier model
Each child got 3/4 (three-quarters) of a roti. Cut each of the 3 rotis into 4 equal pieces (quarters). You now have 3 × 4 = 12 small pieces in total. Divide those 12 pieces equally among the 4 children (12 ÷ 4 = 3). Each child gets 3 quarter-sized pieces …

I’m in Class 8. My friend says one eighth of a roti is bigger than one quarter because 8 is bigger than 4. Our rotis are the same size. Is my friend right?

Frontier models

GPT-6.2 AstraFrontier model
No. One quarter of a roti is twice as big as one eighth. Imagine cutting a roti into 4 equal pieces. Each piece is one quarter. Now cut each piece in half. You have 8 equal pieces, and each is one eighth. It takes two eighths to make the quarter you started with. …

Text only

One quarter (1/4): You cut the roti into 4 equal pieces. Each slice is 0.25 (or 25%) of the whole roti. One eighth (1/8): You cut an identical roti into 8 equal pieces … each slice is half the size, only 0.125 (or 12.5%) of the roti. … Your friend is incorrect …

No. Since the rotis are the same size, one eighth is smaller than one quarter. The larger denominator means the roti is cut into more equal pieces, so each piece is smaller. Your textbook explains that fractions describe proportions of a whole, so the size of the whole matters. Imagine cutting one roti into 8 equal pieces. One eighth is one of these pieces. One quarter is two of these pieces: 1/8 < 2/8 = 1/4. … Your turn: Two rotis are the same size. Which is bigger: one sixth of a roti or one third of a roti? Why?

The frontier models are strong. They are not in this ecosystem.

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Meta AI in WhatsApp are already in the student's pocket, and their maths is right. What they do not carry is the student's own world. Margin lives inside the learning app that holds all of it, so it starts where a general assistant has to be told.

  • The student's textbook, down to the page
  • The method subject experts wrote and vetted
  • Videos, with the minute that matters
  • Simulations and games for the same idea
  • Lakhs of questions to practise on
  • What comes before this topic, and what to study next

Indian doubt-solving apps

Ask Ved, PhysicsWallah AI Guru, ALLEN Allie, Infinity Learn and Teachmint answer a typed doubt with a written explanation. Some add a follow-up quiz or a guided mode.

Margin puts the textbook page, the picture, the video minute, the lab and the game in the same reply.

Photo solvers

Photomath, Gauth and QANDA turn a photo of a question into worked steps. Their strength is how little a student has to type.

Margin gives one hint when one step is enough, and checks the student can do the next question.

Tutors built around their own lessons

Khanmigo sits beside Khan Academy's material. MATHia checks each step inside its own curriculum. Eedi uses diagnostic questions to find a misconception.

Margin applies the same principle to Indian boards, on the textbook the family already owns.

Large question banks abroad

Roboguru in Indonesia, and Yuanfudao and Zuoyebang in China, match a question against a very large solved library.

Margin adds a teaching order and a next step on top of the match.

212

products and programmes studied, in India and abroad. We did not find one that puts the textbook's method, the page, the video minute, the simulation, the game and the practice into a single reply.

Beyond one answer

Others answer the question. Margin is built to take her through the week.

Every tutor above got the answers right. The difference is in everything around the answer: how each product opens, what it gives back, whether it knows her book and her school, what brings her back, and what the family sees.

Where Margin is different

Her book, her teacher's way

The NCERT method and page, checked by subject experts; with school notes, the teacher's own steps. The general assistants answer well, but not from her book.

Her week

Homework, timetable and test dates turn into what to do tonight. No product found plans from a school's week.

Her history

Doubts, checks and marks feed spaced review and gap repair, across classes, with the parent's consent.

The app around it

Videos, labs, games, practice and mentors are already in the app. Margin is the way in to all of them, one step at a time.

The family and the school

An honest weekly view for the parent; a class view for the teacher. Built in from the start, not added later.

Two new features

After the doubt: make it stay, and fix what sits under it

A reply clears one doubt on one evening. Two features carry the learning past that evening, and both feed one learning path for each student.

  • Spaced learningMargin comes back after the right number of days: “You asked about this a while ago. Can I ask you a new one?”
  • Gaps in learningFrom the doubts a student asks, Margin finds the earlier idea that is missing and leads the student through a short path that fixes it.
Spaced learning

Come back with a new question, on the right day.

A doubt cleared tonight fades unless it is used again. Asking for it, a few days later and in a new form, is one of the two study methods with the strongest evidence.

What goes on the list

Every idea a student asked about and then answered the closing question on. A wrong answer brings it back sooner.

Always a new question

A fresh question on the same idea from the vetted bank, never the one already seen. A repeat tests memory of the answer. A new one tests the idea.

On the right day

First return after two or three days, then about a week, then two to three weeks. A right answer stretches the gap. A wrong one shortens it and offers help.

Inside the next visit

One to three questions when the student next opens Margin, mixed across topics. At most one reminder, and only one that names the idea.

Margin decides when it is kept

An idea leaves the list after three right answers on three separate days. The student does not choose when to stop.

The schedule for one idea

No study has fixed the best days for children of 9 to 13 in an app. Margin starts from the rule research gives, and tunes it on what its own students remember.

Day 0The doubtReply, then the closing question
Day 2New question 1Right: the gap grows
Day 9New question 2Mixed with other ideas
Day 25New question 3Three right: kept

A wrong answer on any return: back in two days, with the common mix-up or a short path offered first.

The days shown are an example. Before an exam, each gap is kept to roughly a tenth to a fifth of the time left. That is our reading of the range in which one review best held facts until a test a few weeks to months away (Cepeda and others, 2008).

What the evidence shows

Spacing and testing are rated the two most useful of ten study methods (Dunlosky and others, 2013). In maths the effect is real and smaller than in learning facts.

61% vs 38%

on a surprise test a month later, for practice that was mixed and spread out, against practice by topic in one block. 54 Grade 7 maths classes.

Rohrer and others, 2020

0.39 to 0.61

gain, in two studies, when 12 maths problems were spread over three sessions a week apart and tested four weeks later. Year 7 pupils who did them in one go felt more sure and remembered less.

Emeny, Hartwig and Rohrer, 2021

0.24

average gain from spacing inside a real maths course, across 27 studies. Smaller than in the lab, and still worth having for a feature that costs little.

Murray, Horner and Göbel, 2025

Less

study on days without a reminder, for children of 10 to 12 who got reminders on some days. Test scores did not rise. This is why the question waits for the next visit.

Nobbe and others, 2024

Limits. For Class 3 children in one study the benefit had faded by six weeks. When students chose for themselves when to stop reviewing, the benefit of reviewing until three right answers disappeared (Rawson and others, 2013). No study yet covers Indian students or school exam scores.

Gaps in learning

Read the doubts for the gap underneath, and fix it at the root.

When a student keeps getting stuck, the cause is often an idea from an earlier class. Margin can find that idea, check it, and lead the student through a short path that repairs it.

The signal is not how many doubts. It is what keeps going wrong.

A student who asks a lot may simply be curious. In tutoring studies, how often students asked questions was not linked to how well they did (Graesser and Person, 1994). Wrong answers are the stronger sign, and Margin collects one after every reply.

What points to a gap

Strongest first. The order is a design judgement; no study ranks these signs.

1

A wrong answer that matches a known mix-up

The closing question's wrong choices are each tied to one mix-up, so a tap says which idea went wrong.

2

The same mix-up again

On a different day, or in a different chapter.

3

Doubts that trace back to one earlier idea

Each chapter's map of what should already be in place, the same map behind “Where this sits”, links new doubts to old ideas.

4

Asking for the answer at once

Skipping the question, or asking for the answer before trying, again and again.

One student, ten days

A Class 8 student in percentages. Three doubts, two wrong answers, one idea underneath.

Monday“How do I write 3/4 as a percentage?” Closing question: chose 25% for 2/5
Wednesday“Why is 0.6 the same as 60%?” Right after the reply
Saturday“Is 7/20 more than 30%?” Said no, as 7 is less than 30
All three needA fraction with 100 below that is equal to the one given

Equivalent fractions, from earlier classes.

Check before naming it“Before we go on, can I check one thing?”

Two quick questions on the earlier idea. One is missed: the gap is confirmed. Both right: no gap is named, and Margin keeps teaching percentages.

Example. Margin names a gap only on two or more separate signs, one of them a question on the earlier idea itself. Careless slips are common: even a well-built adaptive system finds about one answer in five is a slip (ALEKS, Cosyn and others, 2013).

The micro learning path

Once a gap is confirmed, Margin builds a short path for this student and this gap. It is offered, with the reason, and the student can start now or later.

Strengthen: equivalent fractionsAbout 12 minutes · 4 steps · Why this: three of your last four percentage doubts went back to it
  1. WatchThe two-minute clip on making equal fractions, with one question after it.
  2. Try itThe fraction wall. Predict first, then split the pieces and see.
  3. PlayOne round of matching equal fractions, against the clock.
  4. Follow-up questionTwo new questions, no help. Then back to “Is 7/20 more than 30%?”

When the path is done, the idea goes on the spaced list, so it comes back in a few days.

The steps vary

A gap that is one mix-up may need only the correction and three questions. A missing idea may need all four steps. What does not vary is the end: a question answered without help.

Practice is the core

The strong results in India came from work pitched at the child's level. No trial shows that a video, a game and a simulation together beat a short run of practice, so those steps can be skipped.

Vetted, not guessed

The gap is read from wrong answers that experts have mapped to mix-ups. A model guessing alone is not reliable enough: in one 2026 test, nine models predicted how a known mix-up would show up on a new problem only 40% of the time.

MalruleLib, 2026

What the evidence shows

Finding where a student is and teaching from there is the best-tested idea in Indian education technology.

+0.37

in maths after four and a half months of Mindspark, which reads each student's errors and teaches at their level. 619 students in Classes 6 to 9 in Delhi.

Muralidharan, Singh and Ganimian, 2019

+0.33 to 0.44

for Khan Academy practice at the student's level in Uttar Pradesh schools, 5,535 students. The gains came with set lab time.

NBER working paper 34683, 2026

0.05

is what letting learners choose their own path adds, across studies of learning software. The path should come from Margin, with the reason shown.

Karich, Burns and Maki, 2014

These are standard deviations. The India trials cannot separate finding the gap from the extra practice time, and none used doubts in a chat as the signal. Whether doubt text adds anything over wrong answers is not yet known.

One learning path, on the home screen

Both features feed one path for each student, shown as cards.

Over weeks, Margin learns what a student has kept, what is due again and what is missing underneath. The home screen turns that into the next few steps.

Good evening, RiyaClass 8 · MathsExample
Review · 2 minFractions and percentagesYou learned this 6 days ago. Two new questions.Start
Fix a gap · 12 minEquivalent fractionsWhy: three of your last four percentage doubts went back to it.Continue, step 3 of 4
Next in your chapterDiscount on the marked priceComes after what you have done in profit and loss.
Ask a doubt

Three cards at most

One review, one gap, one next step. A child does not choose well among many, and the top place gets used most.

Always say why

Each card states the reason in the student's terms. Showing students what the system thinks they know improved learning in a trial with Class 7 and 8 pupils (Long and Aleven, 2017).

Margin sets the path, the student sets the pace

What is due and what is missing comes from Margin. Which card to do first, and when, is the student's choice.

The parent sees the same path

The weekly view shows ideas kept, a gap being fixed and what is next. In the India trials, an adult's routine around the work mattered as much as the software.

Judged on what sticks

Success is a question on the same idea answered right a week or a month later, without help. Not taps, not streaks.

What it takes to build

Most of the parts exist already. The new piece is a record of each student's ideas over time.

Tag every doubt

Each doubt and each closing answer is stored against the chapter's ideas and, for wrong answers, the mix-up chosen.

Map what comes before

For each idea, the earlier ideas it needs. The chapter maps behind “Where this sits” are the start.

Grow the question bank

Several vetted questions per idea, so every return asks something new. Each wrong option names its mix-up.

A simple model first

A per-idea estimate of what the student knows, updated after each answer. Simple models do as well as deep ones at this scale (Gervet and others, 2020).

Cost stays low: review questions and path steps come from the vetted bank, so most need no model at all, and the search for gaps can run once a night.

Children's data. India's data protection rules require a parent's verifiable consent for under-18s and bar “tracking or behavioural monitoring of children”, with an exemption for educational institutions that may not cover an app. They apply from about 13 May 2027. A record of what a child knows should be used for learning only, named in the parent's consent, and checked with a lawyer before launch.

A reason for the family to trust it.

The student uses Margin. The parent pays for it, and wants to know it is working. An opt-in weekly view gives the parent that answer.

For the parent

“Did the help actually help?”

A weekly view of what the child asked, how many doubts, how much time, which ideas came back and what the child then did without help. Any answer can be opened beside the textbook method it came from.

What earns trust. One change a parent can recognise. Minutes and counts are context. What the child did alone is the proof.

The view is opt-in, and can be switched off at any time. It is being added next.

Four ways the cost comes down

Reuse vetted answers

A question that has been answered and checked once is served from the bank the next time it is asked. First-time answers can take a little longer.

₹3.45 to ₹1.95 a doubt at 60% coverage

Cache what repeats

The chapter, the method and the instructions are the same for every student. They are sent once and reused at a fraction of the price.

₹2.10 a reply becomes ₹1.11. Already on.

Send less Already implemented

Most of a reply's cost is what the model has to read. Sending only the pages that matter, and not the chapter, cuts the largest part of the bill.

Reading is 79% of a reply's cost today

Prepare ahead

The questions a chapter always raises are answered, vetted and stored before exam season, in batches at lower prices, so peak nights are mostly lookups.

margin

Students come with something due. Margin gets them through it, and gives them a reason to come back.

  • Why they come: a question that is due, then understanding, then the test.
  • What it should feel like: the favourite teacher who also knows her week. Useful in a minute, never a dead end, one next step at a time.
  • Why they return: what is due, fading, underneath and coming. It grows as the school, teacher and parent join.
  • Why it is different: others answer the question. Margin holds her book, her week and her history, inside an app that already has the videos, games and mentors.
Screens are prototypes; names, marks and times are examples. Quoted replies are from the matched test of 18 November 2026. Market and research facts were checked between 16 and 25 November 2026; most product facts are the companies' own descriptions. The rules, loops and measures are recommendations.
